metrics.label: Baltic Capesize Index
metrics.blurb: The Capesize component of the Baltic Dry Index. The most volatile part, and effectively a bet on Chinese steel production.

metrics.label: Baltic Panamax Index
metrics.blurb: The Panamax component. Coal and grain rather than iron ore, so it follows harvests and power demand more than steel.

metrics.label: Baltic Supramax Index
metrics.blurb: The Supramax component. These ships have their own cranes and serve smaller ports, so it reflects broad trade rather than one commodity.

metrics.label: Baltic Dry Index
metrics.blurb: The Baltic Exchange's headline dry bulk freight index. Published late afternoon London time, so a morning brief shows the previous session.

metrics.label: VLSFO Singapore
metrics.blurb: Price of the main low-sulphur marine fuel at the world's biggest bunker port.

metrics.label: VLSFO Rotterdam
metrics.blurb: The same fuel in Europe's biggest bunker port.

metrics.label: VLSFO Fujairah
metrics.blurb: The Middle East bunker hub, where most VLCC voyages refuel.

metrics.label: Diesel crack vs Brent
metrics.blurb: Roughly what a refinery makes turning a barrel of crude into diesel. Computed as the gasoil price converted to barrels minus Brent. Fat margins make refineries run hard, which creates product tanker cargo.

metrics.label: Brent–WTI spread

brief.text:
The clearest signal in today's data is in bunkers — the fuel ships burn. VLSFO (very low sulphur fuel oil, the main grade for most vessels) jumped in Asia and the Gulf today: Singapore at $882.50 a tonne, up $60.50 or 7.4%, Fujairah at $856.50, up $34.00 or 4.1%, and Rotterdam at $743.50, up $26.00 or 3.6%. Houston was the odd one out at $737.00, down $2.00. For anyone pricing a voyage, that widens the East–West fuel gap sharply and raises the cost of bunkering in Singapore or Fujairah versus the US Gulf. The data here does not show why the Asian and Gulf prices moved that much.

It is notable because crude went the other way: Brent was $95.84 today, down $1.04 or 1.1%, while WTI was $88.92, up $0.18, leaving a Brent–WTI spread of $6.92. Gasoil was $4.31 a gallon, up 0.5%, gasoline $2.63, down 1.4%, and Henry Hub gas $3.24, down 2.9%. No freight index has refreshed today. On Friday 13 November the Baltic Dry Index — the benchmark for bulk cargo freight — stood at 2,980 points, unchanged; the Capesize index (Capesize being the largest dry bulk ships, typically iron ore and coal) was 4,719, down 117 or 2.4%; Panamax was 2,118, up 1; Supramax 1,836, up 26. The tanker ETF BWET closed Friday at $618.68, up 6.3%. All tanker and gas TCEs — time charter equivalent, the daily earnings a voyage delivers to an owner — are five to ten sessions old and tell you nothing about today.

Running stories: Hormuz developed today, with a report that Gulf oil exports are recovering but vessel traffic through the strait remains roughly 65% below pre-conflict levels. The newbuilding wave added another datapoint — Volare Shipping filed an acquisition of a VLCC newbuild. Shadow-fleet sanctions, Russian diesel restrictions, US port fees on Chinese-built ships and Black Sea attacks had no news today and are unchanged. Separately, an asphalt tanker struck and sank a docked river cruise ship in New Orleans on Friday, with 32 hospitalised.

Watch two things. First, whether Asian and Gulf VLSFO hold these levels or converge back toward Houston, since that directly changes voyage economics. Second, whether Monday's Baltic prints follow Friday's soft Capesize number or Friday's firmer tanker ETF move.

storylines.title: Attacks and blockade enforcement around Hormuz
storylines.what: Attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz have continued into November, with a Sinokor VLCC struck and four crew injured. Greenpeace has identified 540 possible oil spills across the Gulf, Hormuz and Arabian Sea since the US-Iran war began on 28 February.
storylines.why_it_matters: Hull strikes and crew-safety concerns raise war-risk premiums for Arabian Gulf liftings and shrink the pool of willing owners; depressed transit volumes reshape crude and product ton-miles.
storylines.latest: Reported today that global oil markets are starting to recover from the Iran war but Hormuz shipping remains severely disrupted, with vessel traffic roughly 65% below pre-conflict levels.
sources: Gulf Oil Exports Recover as Hormuz Shipping Struggles

storylines.title: Sanctions and evasion in the shadow fleet
storylines.what: US sanctions have expanded across Cuban maritime entities and Iranian false-flag registry networks, while the dark fleet is described as a parallel fleet that has tripled since 2022. The US Treasury may now allow companies to buy sanctioned vessels and return them to legitimate trade case by case.
storylines.why_it_matters: Registry fraud and designations force charterers and insurers to re-verify documents and positions; a licensing route back to legitimate trade could return tonnage to the compliant fleet.

storylines.title: Russian diesel flows and export restrictions
storylines.what: A reported US-Russia arrangement on extra diesel for the US market has met political opposition, while Russia has extended a ban on most diesel exports to end-January. A tanker carrying Russian diesel that had signalled the US turned around off the US East Coast.
storylines.why_it_matters: Diesel export restrictions and any reopened Atlantic route reshape clean product tanker ton-miles and MR and LR employment.

storylines.title: Wave of newbuilding orders
storylines.what: COSCO Shipping Development has ordered 16 VLCCs worth 13.43 billion yuan ($2.01bn), and Teekay Tankers has ordered four more newbuildings, lifting its programme to six ships worth $525.9m. Contracting activity is reported elevated across wet and dry sectors, and Chinese yards are expanding capacity for container ship orders.
storylines.why_it_matters: Large orderbook additions change future crude, product and dry bulk supply and shape secondhand values and recycling decisions.
storylines.latest: Volare Shipping Ltd. filed an acquisition of a VLCC newbuild, and Chinese yards are reported to be building capacity to meet container ship orders.

storylines.why_it_matters: The fees, if reinstated, would change the cost of deploying Chinese-built tonnage into US trades and affect chartering preferences across sectors.

storylines.what: COSCO Shipping Development has ordered 16 VLCCs worth 13.43 billion yuan ($2.01bn), and Teekay Tankers has ordered four more newbuildings, lifting its programme to six ships worth $525.9m. Contracting activity is reported elevated across wet and dry sectors, and Chinese yards are expanding capacity for container ship orders.
storylines.why_it_matters: Large orderbook additions change future crude, product and dry bulk supply and shape secondhand values and recycling decisions.
storylines.latest: Volare Shipping Ltd. filed an acquisition of a VLCC newbuild, and Chinese yards are reported to be building capacity to meet container ship orders.

storylines.title: US port fees on Chinese-built and Chinese-operated ships
storylines.what: The US administration has formally extended its suspension of port fees targeting Chinese-built and Chinese-operated vessels for another two months while trade talks continue.
storylines.why_it_matters: The fees, if reinstated, would change the cost of deploying Chinese-built tonnage into US trades and affect chartering preferences across sectors.

storylines.title: Attacks on shipping in the Black Sea and Baltic
storylines.what: A Greek container ship sank after being hit by naval drones off Bulgaria, and Russia says its forces hit three cargo vessels it claims carried military goods for Ukraine. Finland's military said it detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Baltic Sea on Wednesday, while describing the regional security situation as stable.
storylines.why_it_matters: Strikes on ships and port infrastructure threaten grain and dry bulk loadings and add insurance and routing costs for any vessel calling in the region.
